## 2026-11-06 — #150: is Tsukida's apostrophe really a glottal stop? (maintainer asked)

*"are we absolutely sure that our Seediq data has glottal stops in it? We aren't misrecognizing something?"* Checked:
the character is real — every Seediq-word apostrophe in the PDF text layer is U+0027 (81; italic example font), English quotes
are curly U+2018/2019 (80/84). Tsukida never says what it is ("glottal", "orthography", "apostrophe", "phoneme",
"consonant": 0 hits in pp. 69–79); the ʔ reading is the PR's. 12 words: 35 at word/morpheme start before a vowel ('u ×22…),
9 inside (se'diq ×5, pena'ah ×3, tege'ima). Ortho94 and Ortho113 Seediq both have no glottal letter. Bank references (other
sources; context only) write ≤0.01% apostrophes and spell the same words se'diq→seediq/seejiq/sediq, pena'ah→pnaah,
tege'ima→tgeima, 'u→o/u, 'uyas→uyas. Evidence added to the glottal card (page v4); card still open.

## 2026-10-17 — Poinsot round 2: file layout and dialect mapping RULED (in chat)

Maintainer (chat, verbatim): *"We are going to create separate files for S, N, F, Z, T, and Xiuguluan (which is everything that
isn't marked S, N, F, Z, or T). Z is going to be marked as Sakizaya, not as Amis. Note that this means that there should be two
folders within the XML folder: one named Sakizaya and holding the Sakizaya xmls, and one named Amis and holding the other XML
files. For each dialect, we will have two files: one for head words and one for example sentences. For now, N and S will both be
marked as Southern dialect. T and F will both be marked Xiuguluan. Z is Sakizaya, so the dialect is also Sakizaya. For items
marked with more than one dialect, that item should go into the appropriate files for each dialect. So something "S-F" will
appear in a S file and a F file. Something marked "F-Z" would appear in an F dialect file and a Sakizaya file. Where a reading is
marked as specific to one dialect, there should be an entry in the appropriate dizlex [dialect] file for specifically that reading.
Borrowings should be marked in the appropriate note attribute as an "X borrowing" where "X" is the name of the language."*
Tests first: *"Please start by writing appropriate tests for these decisions"* — listed: every item in a dialect file was tagged
with that dialect; a dialect-specific reading does not appear for other dialects; head-word tag counts per dialect roughly match
headword-file entry counts; Chinese translations contain Chinese characters and never contiguous Latin-letter words; Amis/Sakizaya

## 2026-10-15 (round 62) — can steps 3 and 7 be dropped?

**Asked:** *"Can we drop steps 3 and 7 entirely? It seems that step 10 renders them superfluous.
Presumably the square brackets don't affect the other steps before step 10 anyway??"* ·
*"Maybe it affects step 6?"*

**Answer (facts):** neither runs in the build (`generate_xml.sh` runs only transcribe_chapter5,
build_xml + shared tools); `finalize_source_inventory.py` cannot be re-run (Apple Vision input
absent); committed inventory has 0 brackets in any Seediq line (353 rows). Step 3 runs *before*
steps 5 and 6 inside that script; step 10 runs later, in build_xml. Without step 3 a free-standing
bracket token would break step 6's whitespace pairing (fallback, else the script stops on an
alignment error); a bracket before `*` would hide an ungrammatical example from step 5 (0 such

## 2026-09-11 (round 46) — POL-047 split, inline infix glosses, and a withdrawn finding

**POL-047 split, done.** `CodeAndDocs/generate_xml.sh` is now THE entry point and runs
**no validator**; `CodeAndDocs/validate.sh` runs every check and writes **nothing** under
`XML/` (its output goes to the gitignored `qc-output/`). `run_qc_pipeline.sh` is deleted,
`scripts/reproduce.sh` drives the two in turn. Verified mechanically: zero validator
references in the build, zero build-tool references in the validator, canonical step
order, idempotent, and `git status` clean after a re-run. `generate_xml.sh` also rewrites
`provenance.json` itself, so POL-052 can no longer go stale by omission.

**Inline infix glosses, done.** `AF<完成貌>-吃`, not `AF-<完成貌>-吃`. **V153 goes 26 → 8.**

The rule needed more care than "always inline". A blanket change would have broken the
cases that currently pass, because two shapes occur:

| form | source gloss | why |
|---|---|---|
| `m-un-ekan` | `AF-完成貌-吃` | 3 form pieces, 3 gloss pieces — one hyphen too many, so merge: `AF<完成貌>-吃` |
| `q-um-erac` | `抓-AF` | 3 form pieces, 2 gloss pieces — the root is **discontinuous** (`q…erac` is one morpheme), so there was never a spare piece; wrap only: `抓-<AF>` |

So: wrap, then merge **only while** the gloss claims more pieces than the form has. All
nine shapes I tested now count correctly, and V062 (infix M needs an angle gloss) still
passes.

### 🔴 A finding of mine, withdrawn

Earlier rounds listed "make `maha-ku`/`musa-ku`/`mpuuyas-ku` consistent with the 26
`m-aha-`/`m-usa-`/`mpu-uyas-` spellings elsewhere". **That was wrong.** Before
dispositioning the remaining V153 I read the scan, and Chang is inconsistent himself:

- printed p. 144: **23b** `m-aha-ku`, **24b** `maha-ku`
- printed p. 144/145: **23a/24a** `mpu-uyas-ku`, **25a** `mpuuyas-ku`
- printed p. 145: **26a** `m-usa-ku`, **26b** `musa-ku` — the same word in adjacent
  sub-examples of a single pair

The transcription is faithful. Acting on my recommendation would have edited the corpus
away from the printed page, which POL-001 forbids. Withdrawn in the README with the page
evidence. **Worth generalising: "this corpus is internally inconsistent" is not by itself
a defect — check whether the source is inconsistent first.**

### The adjudication gate did its job, twice

`validate.sh` surfaced two things a passing pipeline had been hiding:

1. **`xmllint` exit 127 — command not found.** The old script shelled out to it, so
   `qc_summary.md`'s claim that "all 22 recorded pipeline commands exit zero" could never
   have held in an environment without libxml2-utils. Replaced with
   `CodeAndDocs/check_wellformed.py`, which uses the `lxml` that ships with the documented
   Python. Same class as the `pdfinfo` crash in round 42 — **undeclared external
   dependencies keep turning up in this repo's verification steps.**
2. **A second set of duplicated assertions in `adjudicate_findings.py`**, still demanding
   369 sentences / 1,556 W after dedup reduced them. Deleted rather than updated: the gate
   already requires `audit_source_alignment.py` to have printed `errors=0 warnings=0
   notices=0`, and that script checks every one of those counts against named constants.
   **This is the second duplicate found in that same file** — the FormosanBank commit pin
   was the first, in round 41.

V153 and V154 are now dispositioned. V154's disposition is deliberately **not** a blanket
"retained": it states that four of its rows are the real R312 shifted column, out for
human review, rather than hiding a known defect behind a rule-level pass.

The student's `gloss_review.csv` is **unaffected** by the infix change — it reads the
inventories, not the transformed XML — so the file already sent out stays valid. That is
a payoff from keying the export to the inventory rather than to the published glosses.

### The deliverable: a gloss review round trip

Asked for: XML → CSV with alternating aligned Seediq/gloss rows, for a student to
correct, then consumed back. Built as three pieces in the dev repo:

```
python CodeAndDocs/export_gloss_review.py          # -> gloss_review.csv
```

(the dev repo is a worktree the maintainer cannot conveniently open).

Two design points that were not obvious:
- **One row-pair per source *record*, not per sentence.** A record with optional
  material expands into several sentences sharing one gloss list, and their word
  positions differ. This was not foresight — the first version keyed on sentences and
  **its own round-trip test failed**, on R031, whose word 2 is `m-ekan` in one variant
  and `ka` in the other. Worth remembering for any future review export.
- **Corrections live in their own overlay**, not written back into the inventories, so
  "what the transcription read" and "what review corrected" stay separable — the
  `manual_edits.xml` reasoning. Keyed on (record, word position); a correction whose
  word no longer matches is refused as stale, one matching nothing fails the build.

65 of 312 records carry a triage `flag`. The sharpest is **`adjacent`**: two
neighbouring glosses that concatenate into a word used elsewhere in the corpus
(然+後, 老+人, w+alis). It caught the `bobo na` split that the earlier `substring`
test missed, and flagged one case in my own chapter 5 transcription — `cubeyo hayan`
glossed 從 + 前 — which is *faithful* (the source splits it on p.158 and joins it as
從前 on p.159), so the flag is doing its job on a true pattern with a legitimate
instance. `count_infix` is kept separate: it is the known systematic infix shape being
fixed in the generator, not work for a reviewer.

Round trip verified end to end on R312 (`ka`→∅, `walis`→walis published, then reset),
and the stale-correction guard verified by corrupting a row.

## 2026-09-11 (round 44) — ⏳ chapters 5 and 6 were never in scope

Maintainer asked why chapter 5 (printed pp. 151-159) is absent. Answer: it was never
in scope, and nothing in the repo said so. Commit `7f98cbe` documents the gap; the
extraction itself is **not** done.

**Book structure, read off the restored scan:**

| printed | PDF | chapter | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| 39-53 | 55-69 | 1 導論, 2 phonology | prose, no interlinear examples |
| 54-148 | 70-164 | **3 構詞結構, 4 syntax** | **the corpus** |
| 151-160 | 167-176 | **5 賽德克語的長篇語料** long texts | **not extracted** |
| 161-183 | 177-199 | **6 賽德克語的基本詞彙表** vocabulary | **not extracted** |
| 184-192 | 200-208 | 術語解釋, index, colophon | not corpus data |

(printed + 16 = PDF, constant across all 353 inventory rows.)

**Why, two compounding causes:**
1. `finalize_source_inventory.py`'s own docstring says "Finalize the scan-reviewed
   **chapter 3-4** source inventory". The inventory's `pdf_page` range is 70-164, so
   chapter 5 (PDF 167) is outside it. It was never skipped example-by-example.
2. The extraction is **marker-driven** — all 353 rows carry a numbered marker (`1.`,
   `a.`, `7a.`). Chapter 5 is continuous narrative with **no example numbers at
   all**, so a marker-keyed pass finds nothing there even when pointed at it.

**The lesson worth keeping.** The repo's three completeness claims all *hid* the gap:
README "a complete reviewed inventory of 353 marked source blocks", `qc_summary.md`
"Reviewed all 353 marked blocks in the scanned grammar", and
`audit_source_alignment.py` asserting `len(inventory) == 353`. Every one is true of
the inventory and reads as true of the book. **A completeness check keyed to the
extraction's own output is vacuous about coverage** — it can only confirm the
extraction is complete against itself. Worth asking of every corpus: what is the
source's extent, and does anything compare the extraction against *that*?

**What chapter 5 actually holds** — and it is the most valuable data in the book for
the bank: ~55 Seediq lines, ~40 free translations of **connected narrative**, the
`sumuladuc` 祭耙 ritual account narrated by 傅景賢 (walis wadan) and retold by
錢成鏡 (pawan torih), each sentence glossed word-by-word in `[...]`/`{...}` and
freely translated. Everything published so far is elicited example sentences; this is
the only running text. Caveats for whoever extracts it: the text layer is markedly
more garbled than chapters 3-4 (`m “ usa s叫m.圖umalu`, `A孔阻止風`), and footnotes
are interleaved with the examples — exactly the V137-V139 footnote-leak hazard.

**Chapter 6** is a Mandarin/English/Seediq basic vocabulary list, ~250 entry lines — a
different data type (lexical, like ILRDF_Dicts/Glosbe), so whether the bank wants it
is a separate call.

⏳ **Open for the maintainer:** extract chapter 5? chapter 6? Both need a fresh
marker-free parser, so this is new work rather than a fix.

Incidental confirmation: the colophon (PDF p.208) reads 賽德克語參考語法 / 張永利作,
遠流 2000, series 臺灣南島語言 vol. 6 — corroborating the citation set in round 41.

## 2026-09-11 (round 43) — D2/D3/D4a/D4b/D5 ruled and applied

Commit `4899d43`. Shape **354 S / 1,487 W / 1,971 M** from 369 expanded variants.

**D3 — the coindex subscript is dropped at intake and recorded nowhere.** Reverses
round 42's `FORM/@notes` recording. Stripped in `source_records()`, the point the
reviewed inventory enters the build, so nothing downstream ever sees it; the
`printed_pairs` machinery and all ten `@notes` are gone. Rationale the maintainer
gave for D5 applies here too: the coindexation is recoverable from the
morphosyntactic gloss.

**D2 — brace scope restored.** `{laqi gaga/temi}` alternates `laqi gaga` 'that
child' with `temi`. `clean_form()` deleted braces unconditionally along with the
OCR's gloss-line brackets, flattening the book's one braced example into a
single-word alternation, so both readings kept `laqi` and one published a FORM its
own translation contradicted. Three-part fix: `clean_form()` no longer deletes
braces; `CodeAndDocs/restore_brace_scope.py` (committed, idempotent, refuses to run
if the row is neither the flattened nor the braced text) restores the notation in
the committed inventory, which cannot be regenerated because its Apple Vision
geometry input is untracked (POL-038); and `brace_alternation()` reads the group
generally with the slash as pivot, **raising rather than guessing** on any shape it
cannot read.

**Confirmed, as asked, that the other slashes need no braces.** All **50**
slash-bearing tokens in the included records sit inside a single whitespace token,
**no** alternative contains a space, and **no** slash has whitespace on either
side. R053 is the **only** example line with a brace in the whole 208-page OCR. So
the author's convention holds exactly as described: slash for word-for-word,
braces only when the scope is wider.

**D4a — no change needed, verified.** Each of the 8 records whose parentheses
enclose a starred alternation — `(saya/*ciga/*kusun)`, `(kusun/*ciga)`,
`(ciga/*kusun)`, `(kusun/*saya/*ciga)`, `(ciga/*saya/*kusun)` — already yields
exactly **one** reading: the single unstarred alternative, obligatory. The
parentheses mark the scope of the alternatives and never reach the FORM.

**D4b — verified, and ids corrected to POL-028.** Exactly **53** records carry
optional material and nothing else, each yielding exactly **2** readings: the 53
pairs expected. The split is made on the original tier, so `standardize.py` derives
each reading's standard tier from its own original.

Those readings were running sequentially (`S0031`, `S0032`), which POL-028 forbids:
one base id per source record, further readings taking `-opt`, then `-opt3`,
`-opt4`, and **no `-opt2`** (the second block stays unnumbered so published ids do
not move when a third reading turns up). Now 265 bases, 75 `-opt`, 14
`-opt3`/`-opt4`. Ids are assigned **after** dedup so a merged-away first reading
cannot orphan an `-opt` from its base. W/M ids compose as `S0020-optW01` — the only
published `-opt` corpus (Latham-1862) is a word list with no W tier, so there was
no precedent. `audit_source_alignment.py` gained guards for the id shape, the
absence of `-opt2`, every `-opt` having a base, and W ids composing from the S id.

Numbering per *record* also shrinks the POL-037 exposure: adding or dropping a
reading inside a record no longer renumbers every later sentence. ⏳ The base number
is still positional *across* records — deriving it from the source record id is the
remaining fix.

**D5 — settled.** Dropping the source's focus labels (受事焦點 / 處所焦點 /
參考焦點) is fine; the focus is already carried by the gloss (`-un` PF, `-an` LF,
`s-`/`su-` RF). Recorded in the README rather than left open.

### A ruling landed in parallel that this work had to meet

While I was working, **#254 "dedup requires matching TRANSL"** merged: dedup keys on
meaning as well as words, and same-FORM/**differing**-TRANSL is never deletable
without a human — it should be "merged into one S with `ver="alt"` (POL-025)". That
is exactly what round 42's merge already does, so the corpus passes the new rule
unchanged: **HARD=0, SOFT=0** in both tiers, and the shared
`remove_duplicate_sentences.py` finds nothing left to remove.

It does raise a POL-046 question, now answered in the README: the shared tool
**deletes**, this corpus needs a **merge** (10 of its 15 pairs carry a different
Mandarin rendering, and every pair has a second locator worth keeping), so the dedup
stays corpus-local with the reason recorded. ⏳ Folding the merge behaviour into the
shared tool would be the better long-term answer and belongs in its own `QC/` PR
(POL-049).

`659b96857` → `e0cfa4d36` → `b52377cb3`. I rebuilt and revalidated against each;

## 2026-09-11 (round 40) — Zhang Seediq dev-repo audit: three rulings, one question back

Audit of `/workspace/Formosan-Seediq-Zhang-Reference-Grammar` @ `36d2aa6` against
FormosanBank `57fe30f85`. Report artifact:
https://claude.ai/code/artifact/29403e8c-ab55-44ee-ba62-20a8f08872fe

### Rulings

**1. D3 — coindexation subscript `ᵢ` is stripped from FORM and recorded in
`@notes`.** The source marks binding with subscript `ᵢ` (`yakuᵢ`, `pawanᵢ`,
`kuᵢ`, `naᵢ` in S0094/S0095); the dev repo kept it and waived V116 ×12. Ruled:
strip at intake, move the coindexation into `S/@notes` or `W/@notes`. Rationale
the maintainer accepted: it is the same class of object as the focus labels
`(受事焦點)` the build already drops — the linguist's apparatus, not the Seediq
word. Clears V116 ×12 and the 10 PHON values that read `jaku*`/`pawan*` because
`add_phonology` has no mapping for `ᵢ` (POL-003 unmapped-letter marker), and
un-splits 4 token types in counting/attestation.

**2. D4 — optional-material expansion stands as built.** 273 source records
expand to 369 published sentences: 19 extra from slash alternatives, 53 from
parenthesised optional material (`(ka)`, `(ani sa)`), 24 from both. The 53 are
strings the source never prints — the printed form is `pawan (ka) m-ekan ido`
and we publish both readings. Ruled: **keep all expansions.** Both readings are
grammatical, so both are publishable. Consequence accepted: 4 of the 14
duplicate-sentence groups are manufactured this way (`ruhug-un na tama
sapah-mu` / `… ka sapah-mu` generated twice from R113 and R123, likewise
`ruhug-an` from R119/R124). Distinguish from Shih-Rukai-Adverbial's E149→E144
fold, which was a *starred* clitic, not a bare optional.

**3. G3 cause 1 — an infix gloss is written inline: `AF<完成貌>-吃`, not
`AF-<完成貌>-吃`.** Ruled: inline is house style; the hyphenated form is a
defect in the corpus's `word_gloss_for_xml()`, which always wraps
`gloss_parts[1]` in angle brackets while leaving it as its own hyphen piece.
V153's counting (`_morphemes_implied` vs `_gloss_pieces`) already assumes the
inline shape, so this ratifies the rule rather than changing it. Clears 19 of
the 24 V153 findings. Note the 2-piece cases (`q-um-erac` / `抓-<AF>`) currently
pass V153 only because the double-count cancels the source's own missing gloss
piece — they are not evidence the hyphenated shape is fine. **Worth a POLICIES
entry** so the next glossed corpus does not re-invent it.

### ⏳ OPEN — POL-047 pipeline shape for this corpus

The maintainer deferred pending an answer to: *what is the second `clean_xml`
call buying?* Answered in the same turn (below); decision still outstanding on
whether the dev repo must ship `generate_xml.sh` + `validate.sh` before porting
or whether `run_qc_pipeline.sh` is documented as a permitted deviation. The
FormosanBank commit pin (`3a3c47c22`) goes either way.

**The answer: nothing, structurally — not merely nothing on this data.**
`clean_xml.py` excludes `FORM[@kindOf="standard"]` from its FORM pass
(`QC/cleaning/clean_xml.py:725-727`, comment: "standardize.py owns all cleaning
of the standard tier"), and every `.text =` assignment in `standardize.py`
targets `FORM[@kindOf='standard']` (lines 203, 318-334, 375, 390, and the
create-new-standard path). **The two tools' write-sets are disjoint by
construction**, so a `clean_xml` run placed after `standardize` can see nothing
that `standardize` changed; its other passes (S-level TRANSL, the
quote/glottal attestation correction, translation-language metadata) are
likewise untouched by standardize and were already done by the first call.
Verified empirically: building twice from a clean clone, once in their order
(`clean_xml → standardize → clean_xml → add_phonology`) and once canonically
(one `clean_xml`), gives a **0-line diff**.

It is not free, though. It is a no-op that only becomes non-trivial if POL-002
is violated — so it reads as a safeguard while actually being a latent hazard —
and it doubles the cleaner's per-run reports: their invocation omits
`--warnings_dir`, which defaults to `--corpora_path`, i.e. it would write
`cleaner_warnings.csv` **into the published `XML/` directory** (the known
POL-033 gap), and `html_entities.log` is opened in append mode, so any corpus
with entities gets duplicated rows.

## 2026-09-11 (round 49) — ✅ all 84 cards consumed; two of them were parse bugs

103 verdicts read back from the review page. Two of the notes turned out to
describe **defects**, and fixing those closed 13 groups before any verdict had
to be applied.

### 🔴 A real hyphen lost at a line break — 6 groups, and data beyond them

`pdf_text.append_wrapped` dropped a trailing `-` unconditionally, so a word
genuinely spelt with a hyphen that happened to fall at a line end came back
joined:

```
daughterin-law   wellbehaved   nonThao   snapon   stomachache
helterskelter    SunMoon Lake  riceeel   creepycrawly  smoothedged
```

TeX hyphenates with the same glyph the text uses for a real hyphen, so no rule
over the string can tell `contin-`/`uation` from `daughter-`/`in-law`.

**The book can.** Each of these words is *also* printed somewhere it did not
fall at a break — `daughter-in-law` 16 times, `Pu-Li` 81, `Sun-Moon` 31 — so
`learn_hyphenation` reads every printed line and collects the hyphenated words
that appear whole; `append_wrapped` keeps the hyphen only when the rebuilt word
is one of those. Where the book offers no evidence the hyphen is still assumed
to be TeX's.

```
line-break joins with letters both sides : 5586
  keep the hyphen (attested inline)      : 60   across 39 words
```

The lines must be clustered **by column**. A raw page row spans both columns
and interleaves them, manufacturing hyphenations that were never printed —
that is why the first measurement found 5 and the corrected one found 60.

**Verified against the page for all seven groups.** Six are ours. The seventh
is not: p.687 prints `place whereladders are kept`, space missing mid-line —
Blust's.

### 🔴 "A definition will never consist of just a colon"

9 senses reached the build with a definition of `:` or `=`. Dropped in
`Sense.render`.

### RULED — the 92 verdicts

Recorded in `CodeAndDocs/same-form-rulings.json`, applied by a new step **6c**,
`apply_same_form_rulings.py`. This is what the shared dedup deliberately cannot
touch, because it requires the gloss to match so homophones survive.

```
keep-both    18   two words spelt alike; nothing to do
merge-alt    26   one word, each gloss adding something: one S, the rest
                  joining as ver="alt" TRANSLs (POL-025)
keep-either  18   "Delete one, keep the other. Doesn't matter which."
                  keeps the first — the rule the shared dedup uses
keep-second  16
keep-first   12
merge-notes   1   p.359 `da-rima matilaw`
delete-both   1
```

> "\"(function of /da/- unknown)\" should got into a note. And then they merge,
> no need for ver=alt. Just combine the notes."

Implemented literally: the parenthetical moves off the **survivor** into
`@notes`, the two glosses then coincide, and nothing becomes a variant.
`blust-entry-p0359-s010` is now one TRANSL, `5,000`, with
`notes="function of /da/- unknown"`.

A ruling records the S ids **and** the glosses it was given on, and is
**REFUSED** rather than applied when the build no longer matches — a later
parse fix cannot silently redirect a verdict onto sentences nobody read. 11
verdicts were skipped for exactly that reason; every one of the 11 agrees with
what the rule that closed its group did.

## 2026-09-11 (round 48) — ✅ the gloss key was a literal string; that was the bug

> "A lot of the entries actually seem to be identical, I'm not sure why they
> aren't deduped automatically."

Because the gloss was compared as a **literal string**.
`QC/cleaning/remove_duplicate_sentences.py:176` keyed a TRANSL on its raw
text with runs of whitespace collapsed and nothing else — not case, not
punctuation, not order. A space after a slash was enough to keep two copies
of the same sentence apart.

That shape is right for a FORM, which is language data. It is wrong for a
gloss, which is prose a translator wrote. Blust prints every entry twice —
under its headword and again in the index — typeset independently each time,
so the two copies disagree about presentation without disagreeing about
meaning:

```
spacing around a slash   `was/ were fed`          `was/were fed`
sentence case            `Did you take my money?` `did you take my money?`
a separator swapped      `..., was dressed`       `...; was dressed`
the order of alternates  `move slightly, stir`    `stir, move slightly`
a stray closing quote    `was chewed by someone'` (p.469, the book's own typo)
```

Every one of those reached the maintainer as a card with no answer to give.

### The census that made the call

All 115 open groups, classified mechanically rather than by eye:

```
   7  A. spacing/case/final-stop only
  10  B. same words, different order
  31  C. one word differs
  26  D. 2-3 words differ
   4  E. one side adds a trailing clause
  37  F. different glosses
```

### RULED

Asked how far to normalize and where to put it; the maintainer chose
**spacing + word order**, in the **shared tool**.

`normalize_gloss_for_comparison` in `QC/validation/validate_duplicate_sentences.py`
keys a gloss on its sorted bag of words: letters and digits, with an
apostrophe or hyphen allowed **inside** a word so `don't` and `five-colored`
stay whole; everything else — slash, comma, brackets, a trailing stop, a
stray quote — is a separator. Used by both `sentence_meaning`s and by the
remover's `_transl_key`, which needs the same test for its second job:
a survivor glossed `move slightly, stir` must not collect `stir, move
slightly` back as a `ver="alt"` variant of itself.

**What it costs:** word order stops being meaningful, so `father of the
bride` and `bride of the father` are one key. `or` is left as a word, not a
separator, so `tamed or domesticated` and `tamed, domesticated` still
differ — there is exactly one such pair in the book, and it got a ruling.

**Blast radius, measured before proposing it:**

```
Nowbucyang-Truku-Thesis   same-FORM/diff-gloss groups=1   would newly merge: A=0  B=0
Safolu-Amis-Dictionary    same-FORM/diff-gloss groups=0   would newly merge: A=0  B=0
Virginia_Fey_Dictionary   same-FORM/diff-gloss groups=0   would newly merge: A=0  B=0
```

Zero rows in every corpus that already runs the dedup.

### The individual verdicts, in the maintainer's words

> "These aren't even actually different." — `an-ana-i` p.291
> "These appear to be identical." — `ia-brith` p.326
> "These are the same, just with the two options in the TRANSL reversed."
> — `ia-rimrim` p.410

All three now close on the rule. Nine more are in `RULED`: p.351 s7 and
p.970 e8 keep both; p.289 s4, p.351 e7, p.409 s22, p.416 s19, p.422 s6,
p.445 e3, p.693 e8 merge. Two the new key cannot reach, so they are verdicts
not rules — p.394 (`tamed or domesticated` / `tamed, domesticated`, "These
are actually the same") and p.411 (`of clothes` / `of clothing`, "These
appear to be identical"). p.359 is noted for the merge mechanism:

> "\"(function of /da/- unknown)\" should got into a note. And then they
> merge, no need for ver=alt. Just combine the notes."

### ↩️ One question answered back

> "These have opposite meanings???" — `i-ra-rauriuq` p.422

They are not opposite. `[I]` is Blust's imperative label and `(don't) X` is
his notation for a form that occurs in **both** polarities — **403** TRANSLs
in the book open that way. The entry gloss is the notation; the p.826 record
is the same form written out as a running example. Only 2 groups in the book
pair a `(don't)` entry gloss with a plain example gloss, so no rule. The
card stays open for the merge verdict.

### ❗ 23 definitions end in an unpaired apostrophe — and it is Blust's

Verified against the rendered page: p.469 prints
`k–in–arkar [PFc] was chewed by someone' → karkar:4`. A further 14 are
legitimate `` `…' `` pairs (his TeX-style quotation). Not our parse, so the

## 2026-09-11 (round 47) — ✅ two maintainer patterns close 59 of the 171 duplicate groups

The maintainer read the "One Spelling, Two Meanings" page and gave two rules
plus three individual verdicts. Both rules are now code; the page regenerates
from the build, so it fell from **171 cards to 112**.

### RULED (the maintainer's words)

> "If the FORM notes both contain the word `homograph`, they are homophones,
> keep both."

> "Noticing a pattern: This has a `(PF)`, which it shouldn't. That's
> grammatical category, not a definition."

Plus three single cards: `ama` p.289 sense 4 and p.445 example 3 —
"one word - merge as ver=alt"; p.970 example 8 — "homophones - keep both".

### Pattern 1 — a grammatical label is not a definition

Blust prints the label in its own face (`T11`), and `parse_entries.py` puts
that face in the sense's `label` slot. Two things defeat it:

- a **compound** label is split across spans — `[AFc;` + `PFc]`, `[F;
  atemporal]`, `[C/IT/ PF]`, `[LF; I]` — and the pieces land in the definition
  face instead;
- **printed p.291** is set in a different font family throughout, so even
  simple labels arrive as `T4`.

Either way the label opens the definition, and `clean_xml.py:435` then turns
the square brackets round, so the published TRANSL read `(PF) by oneself`.

The fix is `parse_entries.py`:

```python
LEADING_LABEL = re.compile(r"^\[([A-Z][A-Za-z0-9;,/ ]*)\]\s*")
```

applied in `Sense.render()` after `_lift_comparisons`. Two deliberate
narrowings:

- **anchored, and required to open with a capital** — `[= /qut/] fish bone`
  is an equivalence note, not a label, and stays in the definition;
- **square brackets only**. 24 example translations open with a ROUND-bracket
  English word — `(When) I came ...`, `(They) went around ...` — and a looser
  rule would have eaten them. `(I) drank (it)` is the trap: `(I)` is both a
  Blust label and the English pronoun.

Where the slot already held a label the leading one wins, because it is the
one printed immediately after the form. One case: p.375 sense 8 prints
`f-in-ariw [AFc; PFc] bought ...` with the label split over two spans, and a
stray `[PF]` had taken the slot — now `label='[AFc; PFc]'`.

**24 definitions fixed; the count of definitions opening with a label went
25 → 0.** 6 of the 171 duplicate groups close as a consequence: once the
label leaves, the two glosses are identical and the dedup removes one.

### Pattern 2 — BOTH sides subscripted means two words

`both_marked_homograph()` in `review_same_form_other_gloss.py` settles a group
without a card when **every** member's `FORM/@notes` carries a `Homograph`
note. Measured:

```
ALL members carry a Homograph note : 50
ANY member                         : 59
```

The `both` is what does the work. The 9 one-sided groups are **not**
homophones — the note is about that entry's own root and says nothing about
the pair: `kawi a filhaq` "leaf of a tree" vs "leaves of a tree";
`shan-na-ikahi` "wait awhile" vs "Wait awhile!". They stay open, and the
page's chip for them is renamed **"one side subscripted"**.

### Verified after the rebuild

```

=== Validation summary: 21 files, 0 with issues ===   (validate_xml)
S=16534 tokens=63911 {'entries': 7758, 'examples': 8609, 'texts': 167}
validate_duplicate_sentences: HARD=0, SOFT=165        (was 171)
same-form-other-gloss: 112 groups {'entry': 93, 'example': 10, 'one side subscripted': 9}
```

S 16,540 → 16,534 and tokens 63,917 → 63,911: the six sentences the label fix
made into exact duplicates.

Committed `ff35058` in the dev repo. Page republished at the same URL.

## 2026-09-11 (round 46) — ❗ three corrections, and the dictionary is deduped

### ❗ What I got wrong, and why

**"No corpus uses the shared dedup tool."** Wrong. I grepped
`/workspace/wt-thao-qc`, which is a **sparse checkout with no `Corpora/`
directory at all**. Three corpora call it, two of them dictionaries:

```
Corpora/Virginia_Fey_Dictionary/CodeAndDocs/make_xml.sh:65   --apply  "POL-022 dedup"
Corpora/Safolu-Amis-Dictionary/CodeAndDocs/make_xml.sh:81    --apply  "POL-022 dedup"
Corpora/Nowbucyang-Truku-Thesis/CodeAndDocs/make_xml.sh:64
```

**"The tool would keep the index stub 2,162 of 4,321 times, throwing away the
entry context and sense number."** The right measure is what *differs*, and the
maintainer was right that most of it is nothing:

```
S the tool would delete                      4,518
  gloss identical too - nothing lost         4,318   (95.6%)
  TRANSL differs from the survivor             200   (4.4%)
     of those, a marked homograph pair          80
  carrying an etymology the survivor lacks      38
```

**"The `illustrates` attribute."** There is no such attribute; it is a clause
inside `S/@source`. We add no attributes. `@source` is legal on `S_Type` and
`AUDIO_Type` in the XSD, never on `FORM`.

### The maintainer's rulings

> *"The shared dedup tool really shouldn't be deleting things with the same FORM
> and different TRANSLs anyway. That's going to hit homophones... update the
> shared dedup tool to not dedup unless FORM and TRANSL match at the S level.
> Then... emit HARD errors if FORM and TRANSL match for two different Ss, and
> emit soft ones if FORM matches but TRANSL doesn't."*

**FormosanBank `feature/dedup-requires-matching-transl`** (2 commits):

| | |
|---|---|
| `remove_duplicate_sentences.py` | equivalence is now the base FORM **and** every TRANSL |
| `validate_duplicate_sentences.py` | keyed on FORM so a repeated spelling is still reported; same gloss → HARD where the pipeline dedups, different gloss → SOFT always |

This **supersedes (POL-050)** the old `ver="alt"` merge path: the remover used to
delete the loser and merge its distinct TRANSLs into the survivor. POL-025 is
still honoured, and more simply — a distinct translation cannot be lost to dedup
because the S carrying it is never removed. The test asserting the old behaviour
is rewritten and says so. Two new tests.

> *"We should not include the `See X:N` pointers, even in notes."*

4,278 of them, gone from the XML; all still in `entry-records.json`.

> *"For the etymology notes, we can just delete the one without the etymology
> note first, before deduping."*

`CodeAndDocs/prefer_the_etymology.py`, new and corpus-local, runs as step 6a.
40 entries. Blust's index entry never carries the etymology and his sub-entry
does; the remover keeps the first by `(file, S id)`, which in an alphabetical
dictionary would otherwise discard the etymology about half the time. After 6a
the remover has only interchangeable copies to choose between.

## 2026-09-11 (round 45) — ⚠️ the dedup: the shared tool's keep-rule is wrong here, and the two duplicate classes are not alike

**Maintainer:** *"The dictionary XML should go through a dedup. Both the
dictionary entries and the example sentences. We have shared QC code for that, I
believe. Hunter may already be using it."* and *"Do check those 61 index entries
with no twin."*

### The 61: all gloss differences, none a missing target

```
index entries with no exact form+gloss twin                     61
   the same FORM exists elsewhere, so the GLOSSES differ        61
   the form appears nowhere else (target did not publish)        0
```

So the "probably just an error in the dictionary" case **does not arise**. Every
one is Blust glossing the same form twice in slightly different words:

| form | index printing | main printing |
|---|---|---|
| `h-m-in-adana` | raised; tamed, domesticated | raised; tamed **or** domesticated |
| `ia-brith` | act in a **rational or respectable** manner | act in a **respectable or rational** manner |
| `ia-muqmuq` | be tolerant of **others' faults** | be tolerant of **the shortcomings of others** |
| `ing-karunkun` | walk around it | walk around it**, circumambulate it** |
| `ana-i` | **(I)** (don't) give it | (don't) give it |

Worth discussing, as the maintainer asked, but nothing here is a defect: it is
two printings of one gloss, and the main entry's is usually the fuller.

### ⚠️ The shared tool exists, nothing uses it, and its keep-rule is wrong for us

`QC/cleaning/remove_duplicate_sentences.py` is there; `grep` finds **no corpus**
calling it, Hunter's included. Its determinism rule is *"keep the first
occurrence by (file, S id) sort order"*, which is right when duplicates are
identical. Ours are not — they differ in `source` and in `@notes`.

Blust's dictionary is alphabetical, so a derived form's index entry can be printed
**before or after** the root it belongs to. Measured:

```
duplicate groups                                 4,321
  the tool would keep the MAIN entry             2,159
  the tool would keep the INDEX stub             2,162   <-- loses the sense locator
```

```
kept     blust-entry-p0283-s011   printed p. 283; entry 'ag–ka–kakalay'
dropped  blust-entry-p0434-s001   printed p. 434; entry 'kakalay'; sense 2; bound root marked with bars
```

Run as-is it would discard the entry context and the sense number for **half**
the pairs.

### The two duplicate classes are not the same thing

**Entries — 4,321 groups, genuinely redundant.** An index entry is a *pointer*:
same form, same gloss, plus `notes="See acay:2"`. Blust marks it himself with
`→acay:2`. It carries no linguistic content the main entry lacks. Publishing a
pointer as a sentence is the error; the fix is not to emit it.

**Examples — 34 groups, NOT redundant.** Blust prints the same sentence under two
entries because it illustrates two different words, and the record says which:

```
yaku a pish-tubu   p.280  entry 'a';      illustrates 'a'
yaku a pish-tubu   p.1008 entry 'tubu'; sense 8; illustrates 'pish–tubu'
```

Deduping these deletes the fact that the sentence illustrates `a`. 22 of the 34
have identical English, 12 differ.

### ⏳ Proposal, for the maintainer's call

1. **Entries: fold at build time, do not delete afterwards.** `build_entry_xml.py`
   stops emitting an index entry as its own S and instead records on the main
   entry that the form is also printed at p.N, keeping the variant gloss where it
   differs. Deterministic, reproducible, keeps the sense locator every time, and
   loses nothing — where the tool would keep the wrong twin 2,162 times.
   12,084 → 7,806 entry S.
2. **Examples: leave them.** They are two illustrations, not one sentence twice.
   If they must go, the `illustrates` attribute has to be merged, not dropped.
3. **Then run the shared VALIDATOR** (`validate_duplicate_sentences.py`) in
   `validate.sh` to prove the result is clean, rather than the remover to make it
   clean. That is the shared code doing the job it is good at here.

## 2026-09-11 (round 44) — ✅ one tree, one entry point — and ⏳ one question it surfaced

**Maintainer:** *"Agreed that we should include the XMLs from entries and
examples that we were just creating, plus the five interlinear texts carried
across from Hunter's build. The make_xml.sh should be sure to create both sets of
things. Is that straightforward?"*

Yes — with one hazard and one ordering constraint.

| | |
|---|---|
| **hazard** | `build_xml.write_all()` writes its output directory **atomically**: it builds into a scratch directory and `shutil.rmtree`s the target. Run second it would delete what `build_entry_xml.py` had just written. |
| **constraint** | so `build_xml.py --texts-only` goes **first** (five texts), `build_entry_xml.py` second (it is additive: 12,084 entries + 8,634 examples), and the four shared steps run **once** over the union. |

`generate_entry_xml.sh`, `regenerate_entries.py` and `XML/Thao-entries` are gone.
One entry point again, as POL-047 asks.

```
XML/Thao: 21 files — 8 entries, 8 examples, 5 texts
S 20,885 · tokens 68,514      0 duplicate S ids
validate_xml "No issues found" · validate_text 24,882 SOFT (the known four)
76 tests pass
```

### What the merge actually cost: the two test files

Each assumed it owned a tree.

- **`test_xml.py`** is now the independent check on the *other* pipeline rather
  than a test of the published corpus. It builds `build_xml.py`'s full tree into
  a temporary directory, runs the four shared steps over it through the newly
  factored `regenerate.shared_pipeline()`, asserts, and throws it away. That
  reading of the source is what caught the accent bug and the printed-page bug,
  so none of it is lost.
- **`test_entry_xml.py`** now sees three families of file. Its entry-id and
  entry-locator assertions are scoped to the dictionary's own sentences, and a
  **new test asserts the five texts are present** with their 167 sentences and
  their own id shape — so losing them can never again be silent.

### ⏳ The question the union surfaced: 4,278 index entries

Counting the union turned up **4,448 sentence strings that appear more than
once**, and 4,400 of them are entry–entry. They are not a build artifact: Blust
prints every derived form **twice**, once as a numbered sub-entry under its root
and once as an alphabetical index entry in its own place. Both currently publish.

```
blust-entry-p0280-s007  printed p. 280; entry 'acay'; sense 2
    FORM    an-m-aca-acay
    TRANSL  be dying, be on the verge of death

blust-entry-p0294-s006  printed p. 294; entry 'an–m–aca–acay'
    FORM    an-m-aca-acay
    TRANSL  be dying, be on the verge of death      notes="See acay:2"
```

The index entry carries **no linguistic content the main entry does not** — same
form, same gloss, and a pointer back. It is a finding aid.

```
entry S total                                             12,084
  index entries (a `See X:N` pointer, no sense in locator)  4,278
  of those, having an exact form+gloss twin elsewhere       4,217
  index entries with NO twin (would be lost if dropped)        61
if index entries did not publish: 12,084 -> 7,806 S, tokens -4,448
```

POL-022 is the reason this matters: duplicates are SOFT by default, but
*"reference resources (dictionaries, wordlists, grammar example collections) run
a dedup step"*, and where a pipeline declares dedup every duplicate is **HARD**.
A dictionary shipping 4,217 duplicate headwords is squarely what that rule is
about.

Three options, and it is the maintainer's call:

1. **Publish both** — faithful to the printed page; the `source` attribute
   already distinguishes them; accept 4,217 duplicates in a reference resource.
2. **Publish the main entry only**, dropping the 4,217 that have a twin and
   keeping the 61 that do not. 12,084 → 7,867 entries, no duplicates, nothing
   linguistic lost. The index entry's page could be recorded in `@notes`.
3. **Publish both but declare no dedup**, leaving the duplicates SOFT and saying
   in the README why a dictionary has them.

⚠️ Worth knowing before answering: the 61 index entries with no twin mean their
pointer's target did not publish, or its gloss differs. Whichever option is
chosen, those 61 deserve a look — they are the cases where the two printings of
one form do not agree.

## 2026-09-11 (round 43) — ⏳ WHICH TREE SHIPS: the evidence, and a recommendation

The maintainer asked what the consequences are. Measured, not estimated, with
`QC.corpus_counts.count_words` — the counter the statistics CSVs and the
token-comparison CI use.

```
                                        S       tokens
Hunter dictionary (examples)         8,630      53,136
Hunter interlinear texts               167       2,542
entries tree: headword entries      12,084      12,823
entries tree: examples               8,634      53,149
```

### The fact that settles most of it

**`XML/Thao-entries` contains no interlinear texts.** 16 files, all `entries` or
`examples`; the five texts exist only in `XML/Thao`. Shipping the entries tree
alone drops all five — 167 sentences and every one of the 2,542 interlinear word
forms, which is the only running Thao prose in the book.

And `XML/Thao` alone drops the 12,084 headword entries, which is the material the
rights ruling of 2026-09-10 explicitly covers: *"It's for the linguistic material
in the book. So words + definitions are very much part of our scope."*

So neither tree is publishable on its own.

### Shipping both side by side

```
example FORMs shared between the two example sets        8,590
sentences that would be published TWICE                  8,621
both trees together              S = 29,515   tokens = 121,650
union (entries + examples + texts) S = 20,885 tokens =  68,514
```

A **78% token overcount**, feeding `statistics/*_corpora_stats.csv`, the growth
graph and the token-comparison CI — none of which can tell that the same sentence
arrived down two pipelines. And POL-022 names the case directly: duplicates are
SOFT by default, but *"reference resources (dictionaries, wordlists, grammar
example collections) run a dedup step"*, and where the pipeline declares dedup
every duplicate becomes **HARD**. A dictionary publishing 8,621 duplicate
sentences is the thing that rule exists to stop.

Two id schemes for one sentence (`blust-dict-p0531-e004` and
`blust-ex-p0531-e004`) is the same problem in POL-037 terms: a reader citing the
corpus has no way to know which is canonical.

### ✅ Recommendation: one tree, the union

Publish `Corpora/Blust-Thao-Dictionary/XML/Thao/` containing

- the **headword entries** from the schema parse (12,084 S)
- the **example sentences** from the schema parse (8,634 S)
- the **five interlinear texts**, carried across from the other pipeline (167 S)

= **20,885 S, 68,514 tokens**, every printed sentence once.

Why the schema parse supplies the examples rather than Hunter's stream: it is the
one that carries the entry each example belongs to, so every example has a
locator naming its headword, sense and printed page; it has absorbed all 28 slash
rulings and all 20 entry rulings; and the two now disagree on only 19 of 8,600
example sentences. Hunter's `build_xml.py` still runs, because it is what
produces the five texts — nothing is thrown away, and `extract_source.py` remains
the independent check on the parse that found the accent bug and the printed-page
bug.

⏳ The maintainer's call.

**The guard the maintainer asked for.** A cross-reference is `target:N`, so one
that does not end in a sense number is not finished — hold it open for the next
line. Two in the book, and holding matters for more than the text: the closing
bar arrives on the second line too and is now absorbed rather than read as
opening a new reference.

**🔴 And the guard immediately found a third defect.** With every reference
required to close, exactly two mid-row *opening* bars in the book have no arrow
before them — p.565's, which follows one on the previous line, and **p.370's,
which follows nothing**:

```
4 |pia-dutkhun| [C] lower the head
```

Blust puts bars round a sub-entry's own form when that form is a bound root.
Read as a cross-reference bar, it swept the form, the label and the definition
into a reference, leaving sense 4 of `dutkhun` with `pia-dutkhun [C] lower the`
as its target and no definition at all. A mid-row bar now opens a reference only
if an arrow has already opened one on that line.

reading with the English lifted out of the form. Found mechanically: which
definitionless forms end in two or more words absent from the Thao lexicon.

`data-db-id` is sanitised and keys the store — so a verdict already given locally
is still read back rather than orphaned. `build_review_page.card_id()` does the
sanitising; every generator uses it.

### The four rulings

**1. `ver="alt"` is for a spelling difference, typically one word** — not for two
readings of a sentence. *"So the capu example, for instance, is definitely 2

and `pasa-rima`/`pasay rima`, one word spelt with a hyphen or a space — the case
the maintainer confirmed in the same message. **Zero violations.**

demonstrated to fail when they should:

| test | catches |
|---|---|

| `test_settled_readings_still_hold` | a retired ruling the rules no longer reproduce — the rule regressed |

to the alternating words. Nothing else is superfluous today.

**3. Proper names glossed by a description publish as themselves.** Ruled for

test, because *"I don't want you using your own judgment as part of the
processing, that's not reproducible"*:

> the headword is **capitalised**, AND either the head of the gloss — up to its
> first bracket or clause break — **is the word `name`**, with at most an article
> and three modifiers before it, OR the gloss is Blust's **district formula**, an
> ordinal followed by `district clockwise from`.

169 senses. The 14 distinct gloss-heads it selects are all of that shape: `male
name` (63), `female name` (49), `a lineage name` (7), `a Thao dog name` (4),
`common female name`, `a dog name`, `male personal name`, `place name`,

The capitalisation condition does real work — without it the test also takes

## 2026-09-11 (round 37) — the slash rulings become two rules; the builds converge to 21

**Maintainer:** *"Please consume my responses to 'shared after the slash'.
Integrate the responses to the worklist, etc. Then regenerate any remaining
'shared after the slash' that I haven't explicitly ruled on."*

26 verdicts. With the 13 from the reordering page that is **39 rulings**, and
**two rules reproduce every one of them**.

### Rule 1 — a reading that repeats a word the slash is *alternating*

`resolve_scope` expands a slash by splicing the alternants into what they share.
Right inside one frame; wrong when the alternants are one sentence said another
way, because then there is no frame:

```
printed   ruza pia-biskaw/pia-biskaw sa ruza
spliced   ruza pia-biskaw ruza
```

**Only alternating words count.** My first version counted every repeat, and
that made p.990 `antu yaku sa m-ara, tima/suma painan sa m-ara` look invented
when the sentence simply says `m-ara` twice by itself. Scoping the count to the
alternants also **retires the p.924 curation** — the repeated `cicu a punuq`
there is the sentence's own too, so the rule now leaves it alone unaided.

### Rule 2 — a reading must still contain its own printed part

Shared material is added at one end, so a reading that is neither headed nor
tailed by the part it came from has been **fused**, not shared:

```
printed   a mu-tusi-wak Qariwan/a mu-tusi yaku Qariwan
fused     a mu-tusi-wak yaku Qariwan     <- neither printed part
```

> *"Your proposal required not a shared tail but actually fusing the two forms.
> Make sure you aren't doing that somewhere else."*

It was doing it in two places (p.1022 `tusi` and, partly, p.726 `pitu`). This is
the check that finds it.

### Four curated, from the maintainer's own analysis

| page | ruling |
|---|---|
| p.341 `capu` | the alternation is the whole verb phrase, not `bzu` alone, because `bzu` is an argument of `ma-nasha` |

| p.589 `rima` | `masa-rima/masay rima` — the index entry for the same word, applied by consistency with the two explicit rulings |

## 2026-09-11 (round 35) — 🔴 the misparses are ONE defect: row clustering is too tight

**Maintainer:** *"I wrote some more responses in the worklist. Please consume
and act on responses you haven't addressed yet, then regenerate the worklist."*

Six new notes — `bubu` p.327, `hala` p.395, `dahun` p.353, `balis` p.317,
`haraqhaq` p.397, `bahba` p.314 — each described as a different misparse.
They are **one** defect, and so are the 158 split headers of round 34.

### The cause

Blust sets a line's subscripts, bars, colons, sense numbers and bracketed
labels BELOW its own baseline. `normalized_rows` clusters at 3.1pt, which
strands them on rows of their own:

```
p.317   y = 464.02   T9 pash-balis   T7 nail it!
        y = 467.34   T11 3           T11 [I]
```

The parser saw a form with no number, then a bare `3 [I]`. The same split
hits `|dumdum|:`, `|bariz|₂:`, `qali₁ day; sky; weather` and the subscript in
a cross-reference `→ara₁:3` — **800 lines in all**, in four shapes I had been
fixing one at a time.

None of them needs a special case, because **the two populations do not
overlap**. Over every column of every dictionary page, the gap between one
clustered row and the next is either **3.1–6.8pt** (804 gaps, every one a
split line) or **11.0pt and up** (the real line spacing, 14.9 the mode).
Nothing whatever lies between 6.9 and 8.3.

`Parser._column_lines` re-clusters at **7.5pt**, per column (the two columns'
baselines do not agree) and measured from the line's own first row so a group
cannot creep. `_join_split_headers`, round 34's hand fix for one of the four
shapes, is deleted. `_render` takes the same tolerance, so `ara₁:2` renders
`ara1:2` and not `ara 1:2`.

### Five more defects the same pass exposed

| where | what |
|---|---|
| sense number at margin | ten points of slack let a wrapped translation line beginning with a numeral open a sense. p.887 `shaba` read *"numbering starts at 200"*. Now the page's own body indent |
| label face in a note | `Said to be distinct from /rizit/₁.` sent its subscript to the definition, which ended `... used for houseposts 1`. 3 notes |
| form cited in a definition | set in the sub-entry face, so `(short for haya wa caw)` opened a sense whose whole definition was `)`. 5 definitions |
| alternation slash in the wrong face | p.832 `pasa-rima/pasay rima` — the `/` is set in the translation face, landed in the definition, and the second spelling opened a sense |
| `ETYMOLOGY` stopped at the first `)` | p.925 `(PAN *CekeS \`a slender bamboo: Sinobambusa kunishii (Nakai)')` cut after `(Nakai)` |

Two silent losses made visible: one cross-reference hyphenated across the line
break (p.412 `→kahi-` / `wan:2`) now stays open for the next line, and
`GLOSS?` — Blust's own query, four in the book — no longer falls on the floor
when it follows a root header that has no sense yet.

### Rulings consumed and applied

All six were already in the worklist db and unactioned. Each is a defect on
the printed page, so the record keeps what the page says and the ruling is
applied in `curated-readings.json`:

- **p.280 `acay`** — *"effectively two words"*: `k-in-a-p-acay-an a ayuzi` =
  widow, `k-in-a-p-acay-an a binanau'az` = widower. Two readings.
- **p.381 `filhaq`** — senses 3 and 4 fail to leave the sub-entry face:
  `filhaq a rima rima a filhaq finger`. Two head phrases, words in the other
  order, sharing one definition. Two readings each.
- **p.832 `rima`** — `masa-rima masay rima use the hand for some purpose`: the
  slash is missing and the definition is again in the Thao face. One S, with
  `masay rima` as a `ver="alt"` FORM. **This was the tree's last
  wrong-language finding.**
- **p.887 `shaba`** — `tata wa shaba '100'; tusha wa shaba` / `200`. Two
  examples, 100 and 200. **This was the tree's last example with no
  translation.**
- **p.531 e004** — keep the `(so)`, comma after "table", and the bracketed
  English expands with the bracketed Thao.
- **p.832 `rima`** S08 — the book really does print `1a` twice.

`curated-readings.json` grows an `alternate` key for the `ver="alt"` case.
**`entry-rulings.json` is new**: a finding already ruled is not a question, so
`validate_entries` counts it separately and the worklist stops handing back
answered pages. The ruling is recorded with the words it was given in.

### ⚠️ The two builds were applying different rulings

`THAO_PARTICLES` — the bracketed Thao words that never pair with the English
bracket beside them — lived in `build_entry_xml.py`, so **only the entry build
had the maintainer's ruling**; `expand_source.py` and `build_xml.py` passed no
never-pairs set at all. The same printed example read differently in the two
trees, which is the one thing a comparison must not do. It moves to
`build_xml.py`, which both builders import.

### FormosanBank: `feature/long-parenthetical-never-pairs`

p.445 `a ma-kan (ihu) afu` / *"You will eat some rice (polite invitation to
someone to eat)"* — one parenthetical a side, so they were expanded in step
and the second reading came out **"You will eat some rice polite invitation to
someone to eat"**, a translator's note welded in with its brackets stripped.

Length alone is not the test: `m-ilu (i-say lhalhuzu a wazaqan i-nay)` /
`bathed (in the lake beside the fish trap over there)` is long on both sides
and does pair — an existing test locks that down. What gives p.445 away is the
**mismatch of scale**: one bracketed source WORD against six words of English
about how to use the sentence. `classify` now calls that a note over the
pairing count, the same shape as the rule that already lets an editorial
marker beat it. `split_in_step` asks `classify` rather than the count, so the
two cannot disagree — which also propagates the marker rule, and **six**
expanded records stop welding a note into the "in" reading (p.395, 413, 445,
644, 895, 955). Two regression tests.

### ⏳ New, and needing the maintainer

**Thirteen printed slashes reorder rather than share a frame.** The scope
resolver splices the alternants into what they have in common. That is right
inside one frame and wrong when the two alternants are the same sentence in
another word order, because then there is no frame:

```
printed   ruza pia-biskaw/pia-biskaw sa ruza
reading   ruza pia-biskaw ruza
```

A repeated word is a **detector, not a decision** — p.924 repeats `cicu`
legitimately, because there the slash really does separate two words inside a
shared frame. So these need a call each, on a review page of their own:
`0ea66c53-d4e7…` ("Slashes That Reorder").

They are also most of the **75** example sentences that still differ between
the builds (42 only in Hunter's, 33 only here, 8,557 shared). That 75 is a
**corrected** figure: the 58 reported in round 30 came from a different
measurement. Round 35 moved it by exactly one, the `shaba` split.

(`edfc9bf1a`/`1383d76e5`, `f8c7c538f`/`8c7909fc5`) from an earlier rebase. All
seven together touched **nine files**.

| was | now |
|---|---|
| `explore/entry-grammar` + `fix/policy-conformance` | **one** — `fix/policy-conformance` is already an ancestor of `explore/entry-grammar` |
| 5 parenthetical branches + 2 slash branches | **one** — `feature/parenthetical-and-slash-scope`, cut fresh from current `origin/main`, two commits, 7 files, **1,587 insertions and 0 deletions** |
| `feature/thao-f-labiodental` | still one, **and it is blocked — see below** |

`feature/parenthetical-and-slash-scope` adds only new files plus 91 lines in
`classify_quotes.py`; the three modules are byte-identical to what the dev
build actually ran against. 138 tests in the five affected modules pass on
current main. The seven superseded branches are deleted.

#### The /f/ branch: two corrections to what I told the maintainer

**First: the blast radius was not a new discovery.** I presented it as one.
Round 4 measured the same 8,298 occurrences a day earlier and recorded them.
What I added was only that the dev build depends on the change too.

**Second, and it undoes the first: the port does NOT depend on it.** All 6,066
lines that move in `XML/Thao-entries` are `<PHON kindOf="standard">` and
nothing else - no FORM, no original PHON. Measured:

```
$ git diff XML/Thao-entries/ | grep -c '^+.*<PHON kindOf="standard"'   6066
$ git diff XML/Thao-entries/ | grep -c '^+.*<PHON kindOf="original"'      0
$ git diff XML/Thao-entries/ | grep -c '^+.*<FORM'                        0
```

The corpus builds its ORIGINAL PHON from its own
`CodeAndDocs/orthographies/Blust2003/Thao.tsv`, which is corpus-local and
already says `f → f`. `Ortho113` only ever touches the standard tier. So the
port works either way; what the table decides is whether the corpus's two PHON
tiers agree with each other about this one letter.

`Orthographies/Ortho113/Thao.tsv` is what `add_phonology` reads for the
standard tier of **every** Thao corpus, so on merge these go stale:

```
3,574  ILRDF_Dicts
4,372  ePark (11 sub-corpora)
   88  Presidential_Apologies
   64  Li-Conjunction-Thao
-----
8,298  characters, 14 published files
```

This is the POL-056 lesson again: *"no published data changed"* is a claim
that has to be measured, not assumed.

⏳ **Open for the maintainer, and nothing should wait on it.** The branch is
held. Two questions, in order: (1) is `f → f` right at all - it is a claim
about Thao sourced to Blust pp. 18 and 41, against every other Thao profile in
the repo, which all say `ɸ`; (2) if it is, the four corpora regenerate in the
same change, by full `generate_xml.sh` rerun or an `add_phonology` refresh in
place (PHON is machine-owned, POL-003).

## 2026-09-11 (round 34) — 🔴 the bound-morpheme misparse: a header split across two rows

*"You are misparsing some of the bound morphemes. Not sure why."* — `dumdum`, `haraqhaq`,
`bariz`, `bahba`. Dev `6266406`.

### The cause
A root header's **bars and colon are set about a point and a half below the letters**, and a
homograph subscript lower still, so the 3.1pt row-clustering tolerance can strand them in a row of
their own:

```
y = 293.09   T8  dumdum
y = 296.58   T10 |   T10 |   T7 :
```

The parser then saw a **bare bold word at the column margin**, opened a free-word entry, and the
next row's bar closed it and opened a root that never received a headword. So `dumdum` came out
with **no senses at all** and its derived forms went elsewhere. **158 headers in the book are
split like this** — including the `a` whose subscript the maintainer flagged on the first day, and
`ara`, `ainuz`, `awak`.

The furniture is now rejoined to its header before anything is routed.

```
S02 entry-with-no-senses  12 -> 0, and NO finding replaced it
bariz recovers its homograph 2 · dumdum, haraqhaq, bahba their senses 2,3,4
findings 88 -> 76 · entries with a finding 68 -> 56
```

⚠️ **A mistake caught by the consumption metric**: my first version moved the *whole* furniture
row, but that row may carry the **other column's** text — **817 characters vanished**. Only the
furniture moves now; consumption is back to **100.0%, 0 unaccounted**. This is the second time
that metric has caught a regression the finding counts did not.

### Note on which chip
The maintainer said "sense with no definition" (S03); these were filed under **S02**
"entry with no senses". Worth remembering that the two read alike from the outside — an entry
whose senses all went missing looks the same as one whose sense lost its gloss.

72 tests pass; `validate_xml` **"No issues found" on both trees**; language check still the single
p.832 font failure. Worklist **56**.

## 2026-09-11 (round 31) — the worklist's two patterns

Worklist `6220ad23` (**68** entries). Dev `c4b4070`.

### 🔴 1. A root's subscript is a subscript
*"That's a subscript, because this bound morpheme has a homophone."*

The homograph index on a bound root is set so far below the baseline that **row clustering puts it
on its own row** — 4.2pt down, and **after** the colon:

```
|kazash|  :       y = 398.48
          2       y = 402.66,  x between the closing bar and the colon
```
The homograph test required the entry to have **no sense at all**, and by then the colon had
opened one. So the digit fell into the definition, the root read `": 2"`, and **every such root
looked like "a bound root with its own sense"**. The test now tolerates a sense holding nothing
but punctuation.

```
kazash now reads 1 (free word), 2, 3, 4 (roots) — as printed
S04 77 -> 52 from this alone
```

### 🔴 2. A root with a definition is well-formed, and is not a word
*"if you see a bound morpheme with a definition, followed by a line starting with 2 and a head
word, it's a well-formed entry. We don't put bound morpheme entries in our XML."*

**38 of the remaining 52** are exactly that shape — Blust glosses the root and numbers its derived
forms from 2 — so S04 no longer fires on them. And the root's own gloss is **no longer
published**: only the forms derived from it become S.

```
S04 77 -> 14 · findings 151 -> 88 · entries with a finding 122 -> 68
entry-tree S 20,884 -> 20,787
```

⚠️ Two mistakes of mine while doing it, both caught by re-running the validator: I shadowed the
`numbered` variable S05 and S07 depend on (S07 briefly read **486**), and referenced a loop index
that does not exist in the examples builder. Neither reached a commit.

72 tests pass; `validate_xml` **0 HARD on both trees**, entry tree down to 5 SOFT.

### 🔴 1. "the translation also has a slash-alternation, so the two S-blocks should have distinct translations"
A class: **12 of 93** slash records shared one translation that itself carried a slash, so both
readings said both things — `yakin/yamin` glossed `me/us` on each side.

`QC/utilities/slash_alternatives.resolve_scope` is token-based and language-agnostic, so it
serves the English as well as the Thao. **11 of 12 resolve at medium confidence and are right.**

*I'll peel a banana and eat it* / *I'll husk a peanut and eat it*. **Now 0 records share a slashed
translation.**

⚠️ Pointing the resolver at English exposed **two bugs in it**:
- **Sentence-final punctuation was treated as part of the last alternant.** `Why do you hate
  me/us?` split into `... hate me` and `... hate us?` — the first reading is not a sentence. It
  closes the FRAME; held aside and re-attached to every reading, closing quotes too.
- **Three or more alternants returned the printed parts.** `I called the dog/pig/chicken` gave
  `pig` and `chicken` as bare fragments. The frame is printed once, on the first part.

And one shape it still gets wrong, **recorded rather than papered over**: a three-token
alternation with nothing shared between the sides is ranked below the shortest balanced candidate
and comes out as nonsense at *medium* confidence. The right reading is among the candidates it
rejected. The preference is correct nearly everywhere — including the Thao of that same record —
so the test records the limitation instead of bending the ranking to one case.

Yes — 192 in the published tree — **but 25 were still inline there and 28 here, and both causes
were general**:

  scanner matched the innermost `\(...\)`, which cannot span
  `(lit. I am ripening bananas, (I) put them in)`. **All 25 in the published tree were nested.**
  Depth-counted now, outermost span.
- **Three more were held by the equal-counts pairing rule.** `m-ara (sa) apiq` /
  *"marry off one's son (lit. …)"* — one on each side, so both were called paired. `(sa)` is an
  optional Thao word; `(lit. …)` is about the whole sentence. ⚠️ **Equal counts are a default,
  not a proof** — an editorial marker now beats the count. Genuinely paired material
  (`(sa pagka)` / `(a chair)`) is untouched.


## 2026-09-11 (round 25) — the tilde reverted, the half-words explained, parentheticals retuned

### ⚠️ 7. REVERTED: do not strip the combining tilde
My round-24 change added the tilde to `ACCENTS_TO_STRIP`. **Wrong** — we strip *accents*, and
only where the language's orthography does not attest them. The tilde marks **nasalisation**,
which is a segment, not the source prosody an accent records. `feature/strip-combining-tilde`
deleted, merge removed from `integration/thao-audit`, standard tier keeps `makin-ĩhĩh`.

⚠️ `test_xml.expected_standard` had assumed a blanket "drop every combining mark", which happened
to agree *while* the tilde was stripped. It now mirrors what `standardize.py` actually does:
acute, breve, macron, **and only from vowels**. The test was a second, silent source of the same
wrong assumption.

### 🔴 6c/6g/6l/6o — why a cited Thao word came out cut in half
One mechanism, and it produced both halves of the damage at once. A Thao word cited inside an
English translation, **hyphenated across a printed line break**:

```
p.524  y=205.1  +2.2   'parakaz a lhamic root of the para-'
       y=219.2  +5.4   'kaz tree'
```
`kaz` opened the next row; `translation_on_this_row` was False (new row, no English yet on it), so
it started a **spurious example** `kaz` / "tree" — and the translation lost the rest of its word.
With the indent test, `kaz` is absorbed and `append_wrapped` rejoins `para-` + `kaz`. Same for
`tashtash` (p.440, `The ta-` / `shtash`). Not a separate defect: the same missing signal as the
49 truncations.

### 6b/6e/6f/6i/6j/6n/6p/6q/6r — my artifact's fault, not the data's
These are the **14 I did not change**, and each is correct with its neighbours present:
`k-m-a-tana-i` "Open it!" **is** followed by `k-m-a-tana-i sa pitaw` "Open the door!";
`maka-kikalhi-wak` **is** followed by `a maka-kikalhi-wak i-zaháy a shput…`. The artifact listed
them with no "unchanged" label and no neighbouring context, so they read as mangled. **6d is also
already right** — p0442-e003 `ihu ishtatukdul iza, kalhus uan ihu` and p0442-e004 `kalhus!` are
two separate S, as the maintainer described.

### 6h/6k/6m/6v — yes, the code exists; the threshold was wrong
`QC/utilities/parentheticals.take_notes` moved a parenthetical on an editorial marker or at six
words. Three of the maintainer's calls fell just under:

| parenthetical | words | was | now |
|---|---|---|---|
| `(a floor, etc.)` | 3 | inline | **note** |
| `(response when called by someone)` | 5 | inline | **note** |
| `(further from the speaker than m-in-un-saháy)` | 6 | inline | **note** |
| `(we)` `(to walk)` `(by someone)` `(incl.)` | 1-2 | inline | inline ✅ |

The discriminator is **not length** but whether the parenthesis is grammatically part of the
English or a comment about the example. Five words is where that line falls in this book; `etc.`
marks an elaboration at any length. `feature/parenthetical-note-threshold`, 8 new tests, 31 pass.

⚠️ **Blast radius checked before touching shared code**: `take_notes` has exactly two callers —
the Blust build and `QC/cleaning/suppress_transl_annotations.py`, which **no corpus pipeline
invokes**. No published corpus changes.

68 tests pass across all six suites; validate_xml 0 HARD on both trees.

  (`answer to Shi-ntua ihu? Where did you go?`) — could become its own S block.

## 2026-09-11 (round 24) — six questions, and three of them found real bugs

Artifacts: truncations **`336728b6-2d4e-4595-8092-0cdb5126765b`**, comparison `7d4cc606`,
worklist `6220ad23`. Commits `7402b0f`, `f272a2d`, `aa68a01`, `cf25015`; FormosanBank
`feature/strip-combining-tilde` (`2861f6b17`).

### 1. What actually reaches the XML — the maintainer's assumption was right
Sense numbers, labels and cross-references are **not structural XML**. Measured on the built
tree: labels are prose in `FORM/@notes` (7,690 "Grammatical label: [PF]"), cross-references in
`TRANSL/@notes` (4,375 "See sun:2"), sense numbers only in `S/@source` prose. Etymologies (259)
and homograph indices (81) are in `FORM/@notes`; source notes (1,069) and literal translations
(199) in `TRANSL/@notes`. The schema has `W/@class`/`@sclass` that could carry a label properly
and nothing at all for a cross-reference.

### 2. 🔴 RIGHTS — the recorded scope was WRONG
`source-lock.json` listed "dictionary definitions" among the **exclusions** and
`rights-evidence.json` said the grant covered "texts and example sentences". **It covers the
linguistic material in the book** — maintainer's ruling, 2026-09-11; they hold the
correspondence. Words + definitions are in scope. Corrected in both files (with a note naming
the ruling), and in the README. POL-043 forbids weakening a rights claim from absence of
evidence; this widens one on the rights holder's own statement. **The two XML families stay
separate because they are different kinds of text, not for any rights reason.**

### 3. 🔴 The "repetition glyph" is TeX's TILDE ACCENT
The maintainer's instinct — "a glyph used 4 times in a 1000-page book sounds like a scanner
artifact" — was right, and better than that. TeX's OT1 encoding keeps its accents in the last
font positions: 0x7B endash, 0x7C emdash, 0x7D double acute, **0x7E tilde**, 0x7F dieresis. The
first two were already decoded; the tilde was not. **74 of them on 15 pages, 44 reaching the
published XML inside Thao FORMs.** It is positioned just left of its base exactly like the acute
at 0x13, so the rule already in `join_spans` handles it:

```
*naCuq~    ->  *ñaCuq     PAN *ñaCuq
*qanud~    ->  *qañud     PAN *qañud `drift on a current'
*nam~nam~  ->  *ñamñam    PAN *ñamñam `taste, try; tasty'
makin-~ih~ih  ->  makin-ĩhĩh   a nasalised onomatopoeia
```
Entries 6,519 -> 6,517 (the two `~` pseudo-entries are gone), E11 -> 0, S02 14 -> 12.

**Follow-on, FormosanBank:** `ACCENTS_TO_STRIP` held acute/breve/macron but not the tilde, so
the standard tier kept `ĩ` while stripping the `á` beside it. Added on
`feature/strip-combining-tilde`. No reference orthography lists a tilde letter and no published
standard FORM has one, so **zero existing corpora change**; an orthography that attests one is
protected by the derived keep set. Conservative by construction — `_strip_latin_cluster` strips
only **vowels**, so `ñ` stays a letter and the PAN reconstructions keep theirs.

### 4. Expansion rules, and how they compare
Hunter: optional `(x)` -> `-opt01out`/`-opt01in`; slash -> `-alt01`.. from a curated scope file;
no alternate tier; readings share the TRANSL except 28 that split in step.
**Song-Kanakanavu**: splits `/`, **`;`** *and* `(…)`, **before the standard tier is copied**;
`a`/`b`/`c`-suffixed ids; shares TRANSL; drops cross-record duplicates; excludes bound prefixes.
**NTU**: two separate scripted steps with strict preconditions — optional-parenthetical split
(58 sentences) requires the FORM to have a paren, the translation none, and every paren-bearing
word to be a *whole* parenthetical with a fully parenthesised gloss; slash expansion (1 sentence)
scopes the slash to the **morpheme**, so `pua/mua/mu-lebe` gives `pua-lebe`/`mua-lebe`/`mu-lebe`,
not the naive split. Blust's is closest to Song's; NTU's morpheme-scoped slash rule is the one
worth stealing for the 94 unexpanded examples.

### 5/6. 🔴 The 49 truncated examples — Hunter had 45 of them right
Position separates a wrapped line from a new one: an example **opens** at margin+2, a wrapped
body line is indented to **margin+5**.
```
p.372  pa-shzup-i uan ihu sa falhán sa nak   margin+2.2  OPENS
       a maca Please put a poultice of       margin+5.4  continues
       falhán on my eyes                     margin+5.4  continues
```
⚠️ **Why the existing rule missed it**: `translation_on_this_row` is reset at the top of every
row (`run()`), so it answers "has English appeared *earlier on this line*?" — not "is a
translation open?". The citation had wrapped onto the next line, where it was the *first* span.
Hunter's `translation_started` has the identical one-line limit; what saved him was a **second**
signal, `continuation_x`, which had not been carried over.

The same rule settles **the first defect ever reported here**: p.835 sets an example's
translation in the *definition* face, so it was filed as a sense definition. A definition never
follows an example directly (maintainer's ruling), so an indented body line arriving while an
example is open and untranslated is its translation.

```
single-word examples 49 -> 14, and the 14 are real ("cakaw!" You are greedy!, "minu?" What is it?)
E10 example-with-no-bold-word 38 -> 0 · E07 2 -> 1
findings 193 -> 151 · entries with a finding 154 -> 122 · ZERO new findings
```

Both trees rebuilt; **68 tests pass** across all six suites; validate_xml 0 HARD on both.

### 🔴 The diff caught a bug in MY code


The acute is drawn just *left* of its vowel, so its x-range falls **inside the preceding span**.
Inserting it at the character its x0 landed on put it one letter early. `join_spans` had it right
all along by sorting the overlay 0.5pt earlier; `merge_accent_overlays` now reproduces exactly
that rule one step sooner. Verified on the page for `Alisán`, `baksán`, `Matansún`, `maní`.

## 2026-09-10 (round 21) — the accent, and four rules that were firing on names

"Are you waiting on anything?" No, and I should not have written those two up as open.
The accent fix needed no ruling (it can live entirely in `parse_entries`), and the
false-positive classes were already ruled in the worklist notes. Both done — `35a3e92`.

### 🔴 Blust's stress acute is back
PyMuPDF reports the acute as its own span drawn **on top of** its vowel, so the overlay's
x-range sits **inside** the base span's, defeating every gap measurement downstream — the
headword join `|prev.x1 - span.x0| <= 2.5` closed early and the accent was routed into the
definition.

⚠️ Reordering cannot fix it: `Alis` arrives as **one span**, so moving the overlay in front
would accent the A. The overlay has to go **inside** the span, at the character its x0 lands on.

```
187 headwords now carry an acute (was 0) · strays 139 -> 2
An -> Anáy · falh -> falhán · bak -> baksán · Alis -> Alisán · anan -> ananá
entries/senses/examples UNCHANGED · consumption still 100.0%, 0 unaccounted
```
The consumption metric now merges the printed side the same way, so a merged accent does not
read as a character the parser lost. **Confined to `parse_entries`: `extract_source` and the
published XML are untouched.**

### The four rules, on the maintainer's own rulings
| rule | was | why it was wrong | now |
|---|---|---|---|
| **E01** | 4 | `e` was listed as a letter Thao lacks. Blust describes /e/ and /o/, and all four hits (`Sage`, `Wane`, `iseg`, `tai'eg`) are names or loans | **0** |
| **E02** | 3 | "reads as Thao" meant `tha > eng`, but the English list is the **top 1,000** — `creeper`, `sapientum`, `despises` all score 0, so any trace of Thao won | **0** |
| **E05** | 2 | same, plus proper names counted as Thao: "Kilash finds Ali disgusting" read as **60% Thao** | **0** |
| **E08** | 1 | same | **0** |

Fix: a field reads as Thao only when a **majority** of its tokens are attested Thao, with
**capitalised tokens excluded** — a proper name belongs to both languages equally.

**E03 had to be rebuilt, not relaxed.** Its three hits were real (the book fails to leave the
sub-entry face, so a definition runs into a form) but it caught them only because the English
that ran in contains `e`. Now: ≥3 common English words in a form, or a repeated word. Two
exemptions found by measurement — a printed **slash** is a real alternation
(`cumay a huqi/huqi a cumay`, 11 of them) and `X X` is **reduplication** (`pakish pakish`).
